newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ coalition's poor image to cloud showcase budget.
newsitem.headline: NZ coalition's poor image to cloud showcase budget.

text.p: New Zealand's six-month-old centre-right coalition government hopes its maiden budget due on Thursday will help clear away some of its image problems and bring policy back to the fore.
Internal wrangling, and minor scandals involving Maori MPs from controversial junior government partner New Zealand First, have dominated headlines for half a year.

They have overshadowed what ministers and most observers agree is a relatively populist budget plan, based on expected fiscal surpluses, that is due to hand out NZ$5 billion ($3.42 billion) over three years in new spending and tax cuts.
After years of deficits, and budgets that ate into the hard-won gains of New Zealand's spurt of reforms in the 1980s, the new order aims to use growth to reinforce social policy.
But that upbeat message is barely getting through, opinion polls indicate, and the politician in the spotlight on budget day -- Treasurer Winston Peters -- is a big part of the problem.
"New Zealanders want certainty. They want stability, and they will get it with this coalition budget," he said last week.
It is a message he is working hard to get across.
By law Peters is the man who will deliver the budget at 2.00 p.m. (0200 GMT) on June 26.
By reputation he is the joker in the political pack, the outspoken and rough-edged leader of maverick party NZ First.
After last September's elections he was feted as the man who won the balance of power under a new proportionally-based voting system by charming disgruntled Maori, nationalists and elderly.
By last month his new-wave party's image was tattered and torn by a huge media fuss over his own fracas with a backbench government MP and a stream of allegations about his colleagues.

NZ First's popularity collapsed to 5.0 percent support from 13 percent at the polling booths. Peters fared even worse, with his personal support falling to four percent from 14 in the May opinion poll commissioned by TV3.
Meanwhile, senior coalition partner National, the old-style conservative party led by Prime Minister Jim Bolger, knows its credibility has also been damaged -- implicated by association.

Finance Minister Bill Birch, a veteran of the right-left pendulum politics of decades gone by, partners Peters on fiscal management. Cabinet sources say he has engineered features into the budget that will appeal to right-leaning lobby groups.

In a bid to hark back to the days when New Zealand led the world in deregulation and institutional reform, insiders told Reuters to expect measures to trim the fat from remaining state-owned enterprises and make them work on less capital.
The savings would be re-deployed to underpin the state's new capital expenditure on health, education and housing, thus helping to fulfil New Zealand First's promises as well.
But neither man's task has been made easier by the latest data on the New Zealand economy which show it on the floor of a slowdown with no immediate prospect of bouncing back.

"Flatness in the economy over the last six months means the expected recovery from the bottom of the business cycle has been delayed longer than expected -- but there is ample evidence that stronger growth will resume soon," Birch said last week.

Insiders say the budget will update forecasts to show a dip in the 1997/98 surplus to around NZ$2.0 billion, down from $3.3 billion forecast in December, then further gains in 1998/99 and 1999/2000 as GDP growth picks up from around 2.4 percent now to 4 percent next year.
For business lobby groups, who feel the government's tacit acceptance of a soft landing has left them in economic limbo, Thursday's budget is the less important event of next week.
Manufacturers Federations say that Friday's Monetary Policy Statement from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will be more crucial for industry, as it could herald lower interest rates. ($=NZ$1.46)
